title: A red, metal-rich relic
caption: The lenticular galaxy NGC 1277 in the Perseus Cluster, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
credit: NASA, ESA, and M. Beasley (Instituto de Astrofísica de Canarias)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Glowing galaxies fill this frame, with the large lenticular galaxy NGC 1277 at its center. It is a member of the Perseus Cluster, some 220 million light-years from Earth, which ranks among the most massive objects in the known Universe.

Astronomers have called NGC 1277 a relic of the early Universe, since its stars all seem to have formed about 12 billion years ago. For comparison, the Big Bang is thought to have taken place 13.8 billion years ago. The galaxy holds billions of old, metal-rich stars and many ancient globular clusters, round bundles of stars that circle a galaxy like satellites.

To astronomers, any element heavier than hydrogen and helium counts as a metal. Such elements are forged in massive stars and spread when they explode, so later generations of stars contain more of them. Unusually, most of NGC 1277's globular clusters are red and metal-rich, unlike the blue, metal-poor clusters usually found around galaxies of its size.
scale: The Perseus Cluster lies some 220 million light-years from Earth, according to ESA/Hubble.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed the field in visible light through g, r and z filters at 475, 625 and 850 nm. The color assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Hubble's sharp, deep exposures pick out globular clusters around NGC 1277 that an eye at a telescope could not separate from the galaxy's glow.

explore: Massive galaxies are thought to form in two phases. An early collapse with a burst of star formation makes red, metal-rich clusters, and later gathering of material brings in bluer, metal-poor ones. NGC 1277's red clusters confirm it skipped the second phase, raising questions in a hotly debated field.
